# Galatians 2: Research Notes

**Before you use these notes:**
- I ran out of searches before I could read some of the sites on your list. The netbible.org and bibleodyssey.org notes, oca.org (Orthodox), and Methodist or Pentecostal teachers writing on these specific verses aren't covered. I also found nothing on how prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers read this chapter, so those topics are left out.
- Three pages I read in full can't be tagged with exact citations, so for those I give the URL only. They are the full Enduring Word chapter (which cut off partway through v. 12), the first part of the Precept Austin chapter page, and the StudyLight page on v. 16.
- I quote from Luther and Calvin often below. Where those quotes attack the papacy or Catholics, that is their own polemic, not my assessment.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says this is a second trip to Jerusalem, 14 years after the visit in 1:18. The point is that Paul didn't learn his gospel from the apostles. He notes that Barnabas was well respected in Jerusalem and Titus was a Gentile convert. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/
- Guzik takes this to be the famine-relief visit of Acts 11:27–30. Precept Austin's cross-references give either Acts 11:27–30 or Acts 15:2–4, so which visit this was is still debated. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary
- Boice (quoted at Precept Austin) says chapter 1 stressed Paul's independence from the Twelve. Chapter 2 shows harmony and cooperation with them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary

**v. 2**
- "By revelation" means God told Paul to go; no human summoned him. Guzik thinks the private meeting was a kindness, to avoid embarrassing leaders in public. On "run in vain," he doesn't think Paul feared falling away himself. Paul feared that a conflict, or false teachers encouraged by Jerusalem, might undo his work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/
- Hansen points out that Acts shows Paul being guided by revelation in several ways: through prophets (Acts 11:28; Acts 21:10-11), by the Holy Spirit (Acts 13:2; Acts 16:6-7...), in dream visions. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary
- Wayne Barber reads it the other way round. Paul wasn't seeking the apostles' approval. He is going to find out where they stand on the message of grace. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians_2_commentary-barber

**v. 3**
- The leadership in Jerusalem accepted Titus (a Gentile convert) even though he was not circumcised in accord with the Mosaic Law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/
- Luther (quoted by Guzik) says Paul didn't treat circumcision itself as sinful. He insisted it had no bearing on salvation and must not be forced on Gentiles. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/
- Precept Austin says Paul brought Titus deliberately as a litmus test of true salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary

**v. 4**
- "False brothers" is a severe title. These men didn't see themselves as false, and they may have meant well, but they were dangerous. Stott thinks "came in under false pretenses" means one of two things. Either they never belonged in the church fellowship, or they gate-crashed the private meeting with the apostles. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/
- Paul says "enslave us," not just "enslave the Gentiles." He saw that a compromised gospel wasn't just bondage for the Gentiles, but it was bondage for *everyone* who named the name of Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/

**v. 5**
- Luther (via Guzik) says Paul might have agreed if circumcision had been asked for out of brotherly love. Because it was demanded as necessary for salvation, he refused. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/
- Calvin: Paul accommodated himself to the Jews no farther than was consistent with the doctrine of liberty; and therefore he refused to circumcise Titus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/2-11.html

**v. 6**
- The Jerusalem leaders added nothing to the gospel Paul preached or to the apostolic authority he possessed. Stott (via Guzik) says this isn't disrespect. Paul accepts their office but isn't overawed by the inflated image of them that the false teachers were promoting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/
- The message of a Christian worker is not superior or right because of the greatness of the worker. From the context it is clear that Paul does not mean to degrade the position of the Jerusalem leadership. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik notes the division of mission fields wasn't absolute. "These distinctions were not absolute; each did minister to the other groups." He then quotes Calvin against the papacy: Roman Catholics claim that the Pope is the successor of Peter—but where through history is the Pope's ministry to the Jews? https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary
- Barber on "at work": God caused it to happen that Peter would be assigned the ministry to the circumcised and He caused it to happen and they saw it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians_2_commentary-barber
- GotQuestions argues that Peter's ministry complemented the ministry of Paul: one was sent to the Jews, and one to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7–8). It seems that all church leaders had equal authority. https://www.gotquestions.org/Peter-first-pope.html

**v. 9**
- Guzik identifies the "pillars" as James (the Lord's brother), Peter and John. They approved Paul's ministry knowing he didn't put Gentiles under the Mosaic Law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/
- Leon Hyatt: In the end James, Cephas, and John agreed that Titus was a true believer and did not need to be circumcised. They also agreed that Saul and Barnabas were preaching the same doctrine they were preaching. They had nothing to add. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary

**v. 10**
- The poor here were probably the poor saints in Jerusalem, whom Gentile believers should not forget. Paul later gathered a collection for them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/
- Hyatt reads the request this way: They only asked Paul and Barnabas to be sure they did not preach God's grace in such a way as to eliminate the importance of caring for the poor. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary

**v. 11 — a verse where traditions really differ**
- *Timing.* Constable: Luke did not record this later event in Acts, and we cannot date it exactly. It may have happened shortly after Paul and Barnabas returned from Jerusalem to Antioch or, less likely, after the Jerusalem Council. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/2-11.html
- *Why Paul tells the story.* Bob Deffinbaugh (bible.org) calls it Paul's last historical proof of his independence as an apostle. He also notes that Matthew 18 calls for private correction first, but public correction is necessary where public error has corrupted others. https://bible.org/seriespage/peter%E2%80%99s-capitulation-and-paul%E2%80%99s-correction-galatians-211-21
- *Protestant reading: Paul as Peter's equal, and a case against the papacy.*
  - Barnes says Paul showed that he was equal with Peter in his apostolical authority and dignity.
  - Calvin calls the passage another thunderbolt which strikes the Papacy of Rome.
  - Matthew Henry sees the weakness of the pope's pretence to supremacy and infallibility.
  - Coffman (a Churches of Christ writer) goes furthest. He says Peter committed the most fundamental doctrinal error imaginable.
  - All four: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/2-11.html
- *Catholic reading.* Catholic Answers says Peter wasn't defining doctrine. A pope uses infallibility only when he, as supreme pastor and teaching all the faithful, proclaims *definitively* a doctrine pertaining to faith or morals. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/blog/but-paul-rebuked-peter
  - Peter's actions had to do with matters of discipline, not with issues of faith or morals. Furthermore, the problem was Peter's actions, not his teaching. https://www.catholic.com/tract/papal-infallibility
  - One Catholic Answers guest adds that many scholars see the rebuke as pointing to Peter's authority. https://www.catholic.com/audio/caf/pauls-rebuke-and-peters-infallibility
- *An older interpretation.* The Protestant historian Schaff says some church fathers and Jesuit writers explained the scene as a theatrical performance the apostles staged to refute the Judaizers. He rejects that view. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/hcc1/hcc1.i.IV_1.26.html
  - Calvin also rejects it, and so, he says, did Augustine. Augustine is therefore right in asserting, that this was no previously arranged plan. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/2-11.html

**v. 12**
- Peter already knew Gentiles didn't need to come under the Law. He had learned it from his vision, from the Spirit falling on Gentiles, and from the Jerusalem leaders' agreement (Acts 10–11). Stott, quoting Lightfoot, pictures a shamefaced withdrawal by a timid man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/
- Guzik guesses that the separation happened at the church's shared "love feast," which may have included communion. Precept Austin flags this: (THIS IS CONJECTURE BUT IS POSSIBLE) https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary
- *Who were the "men from James"?* Barber says They said they were from James and that was a lie. He points to the Jerusalem Council's later letter disowning such people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians_2_commentary-barber Bridgeway puts it more cautiously: the men "claimed" James's authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/2-11.html
- Deffinbaugh notes the verbs are in the imperfect tense. This suggests a gradual change in Peter's conduct, rather than a glaring, instantaneous, change. https://bible.org/seriespage/peter%E2%80%99s-capitulation-and-paul%E2%80%99s-correction-galatians-211-21
- Catholic Answers says Peter simply stopped eating meals with Gentiles in order to keep harmony between Jewish and Gentile Chris- tians. https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/peter-in-antioch-and-papal-infallibility

**v. 13**
- Guzik on the hypocrisy: they knew that these Gentile believers were really Christians. Yet, because of the pressure from the certain men from James, they acted like they were not Christians at all." https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary
- Deffinbaugh suggests Barnabas may have felt obliged to the James party. He notes that Barnabas had stood with Paul over Titus, but Paul stood alone against Peter. https://bible.org/seriespage/peter%E2%80%99s-capitulation-and-paul%E2%80%99s-correction-galatians-211-21

**v. 14**
- Guzik: Paul reminded Peter that he didn't keep a kosher diet himself, yet now acted as if he kept those laws all the time. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary
- The commentator quoted at Precept Austin says Peter hadn't given up the gospel in principle. He had "trimmed his sails" to the sudden change of wind that came from Jerusalem. Gentile believers were left with two choices: split the church, or come under the food laws. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary
- Deffinbaugh: The authority for what Paul did was the gospel. https://bible.org/seriespage/peter%E2%80%99s-capitulation-and-paul%E2%80%99s-correction-galatians-211-21

**v. 15**
- Calvin on "Jews by birth": "We are born holy: not certainly by our own merit, but because God hath chosen us to be his people." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/2-15.html
- The commentator at Precept Austin explains it this way: born Jews, and not Gentiles—sinners—denied the obligation of these ordinances by the act of believing on Jesus Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary

**v. 16 — the key verse; real differences here**
- *Traditional reading.* Constable says the verse states justification by faith three times, and the three phrases increase in emphasis. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/2-15.html
- Guzik, quoting Stott, says faith here is not intellectual conviction only, but personal commitment. The expression in the middle of verse 16 is (literally) 'we have believed *into* (*eis*) Christ Jesus.' https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/
- Wuest (via Precept Austin) says "works of the law" means the divine law conceived of as a means of acceptance with God in the case of the sinner who obeys it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary
- *Lutheran.* Luther describes the gospel coming to a despairing conscience with the message that its sins were laid on Christ: In this way are we delivered from sin. In this way are we justified and made heirs of everlasting life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mlg/galatians-2.html
- *Wesleyan.* A Wesley Center article says John Wesley agreed with Luther that the church stands or falls with this doctrine of justification by faith. https://wesley.nnu.edu/arminianism/the-arminian-magazine/revisiting-galatians/
- *What justification means: a difference inside Protestantism.*
  - Bridgeway (evangelical) says God *declares* believers righteous and gives them a righteousness that isn't their own.
  - Barnes (19th-century American Presbyterian) explicitly denies that Christ's righteousness is transferred to believers. For him, God treats believers *as if* they had not sinned, on the ground of Christ's merits.
  - Both: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/2-16.html
- *Restorationist reading: "faith of Christ."* Coffman argues the Greek *pistis Christou* should be translated "faith of Christ," meaning Christ's own faithfulness and obedience. The "faith of Christ" includes both his own trust/faith in the heavenly Father, and his perfect obedience and fidelity in the discharge of his mission of redemption. The doctrine of salvation through faith only is wrong on many counts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/galatians-2.html
  - He also says the "faith in Christ" that saves belongs to someone baptized into Christ. And he limits "works of the law" to Jewish ceremonial law. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/2-16.html

**v. 17**
- The opponents argued that in view of the fact that violation of the law is sin, therefore, abandonment of the law in an effort to be justified in Christ is also Sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary
- The UBS Handbook explains: by abandoning the Law, Jewish Christians became "sinners" in the sense of being outside the Law. Paul's answer to "is Christ then a minister of sin?" is an emphatic no. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/galatians-2-commentary
- Guzik paraphrases Paul's point: "There is *more sin* in trying to find acceptance before God by our law-keeping than there is sin in everyday life as a Christian." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-2/

**v. 18**
- Lovett: The man who tears down a bridge and then rebuilds it, admits he made an awful mistake in tearing it down in the first place. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/galatians-2-commentary
- Bridgeway: the real sin is going back to law-keeping after being justified apart from it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/2-16.html

**v. 19**
- Luther says Paul sets one law against another and lets them fight it out. "I through the law am dead to the law," he opposes one law with another law, and has them fight it out. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/luther_martin/Gal/Gal002.cfm
- Wuest: Paul died to the law by dying with Christ who died under its penalty. The law's demands were satisfied and therefore have no more hold on Paul. Wuest adds that this doesn't make Paul lawless. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary

**v. 20 — differences in emphasis**
- *Lutheran.* Luther says Paul isn't talking about crucifying the flesh here. He means the higher crucifying wherein sin, devil, and death are crucified in Christ and in me. Faith joins the believer to Christ so closely that He and you become as it were one person. Good works are not the cause, but the fruit of righteousness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mlg/galatians-2.html
- An LCMS Bible study draws the pastoral point from Luther: only grace in Christ, crucified and risen, can comfort a terrified conscience. https://resources.lcms.org/reading-study/bible-studies/bible-study-with-luther-galatians-211-20/
- *Baptist and evangelical.* MacArthur: "The true Christian life is not so much a believer's living for Christ as Christ's living through the believer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians_220
- Precept Austin also says the new life is more than imitating Christ: it is "**incarnation**"! https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/galatians-2-commentary
- *A past event or a daily practice?* One writer stresses a completed past event, a union by which His crucifixion positionally becomes my crucifixion. Another, Gutzke, stresses the believer's ongoing "reckoning": He reckons himself to be dead by faith; it is an exercise of faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians_220 ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary
- Hastings' *Great Texts* reads it more ethically. Paul is not describing a merely inward spiritual experience when he says: "I have been crucified with Christ." He is describing his attitude of evangelical fidelity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hastings/galatians/2-20.htm
- *Catholic reading, as reported by a Protestant source.* The Expositor's Greek Testament says the faith in this verse is not the fides formata (Catholics, including Bisping and Reithmayr). *Fides formata* is faith formed by love; the EGT is rejecting the Catholic writers who read the verse that way. I didn't find a Catholic site's own treatment of this verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/galatians/2-20.htm
- Guzik: The focus of this verse isn't the flesh, it is faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary

**v. 21**
- McGee: if there had been any other way to save sinners, then God would have used that method. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-2-commentary
- Adding works to faith has thwarted the efficacy of grace, for the fundamental meaning of grace is that salvation is given free. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/galatians-2-commentary
- Luther (quoted in the Light of Israel commentary) asks: How can I buy for a penny what cost a million dollars? https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/2-20.html
